We have had a few fun evenings playtesting this against eachother at the office

In one of my favorite experiments, I told Fable 5.2 to build an endless, hands-off journey through 3D worlds linked by portals.

25,000 agents created over 450 worlds inspired by books, art, places, all in code.

Play: https://portals-endless-worlds.netlify.app/
Github: https://github.com/emollick/ai-portals

In addition to more serious examples I shared in my post, I had Fable 5.2 build a parody reverse Scooby Doo game where you have to scare away meddling kids. Here is the trailer it made (including the music and sounds) and the game (which is fun) is here: https://i-would-have-gotten-away-with-it.netlify.app/

I had early access to Fable 5.2 for a bit & I think it crosses the line into being a sort of Jagged AGI. Here, I have it launch a business, do academic research, hack hardware, build 3D models & more. I think it is a good illustration of limits & powers: https://www.oneusefulthing.org/p/fable-52-and-jagged-agi

We wanted to do more for the people who’ve been with us the longest. So with Fable 5.2, the longer you’ve been subscribed, the more Fable resets you get.

Release: llm-anthropic 0.31

 Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. I've added them to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this:

 uv tool install llm
llm install llm-anthropic
llm keys set anthropic
# paste key here
llm -m claude-fable-5.2 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle"

 I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh :

 max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine.

blogs.name: Simon Willison's Weblog
blogs.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
blogs.description: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room…
blogs.content:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

 Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

 You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

 The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

 Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

 I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

 Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

 Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

 The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

 How it works

 When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

 We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

 That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

 Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

 When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

 How I built it

 I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

 Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

 There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

 I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

 There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

 Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

 That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

 The research looked good, so I told it:

 Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

 That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

 I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

 I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

 This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

 On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

 From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

 I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

 This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

 what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

 Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

 That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

 each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

 That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

 The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

 Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

 There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

 Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

 At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

 I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

 And since I had one spare device, I then said:

 add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

 Giving Claude Code ears

 I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears .

 Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

 I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

 Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

 I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

 Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

 Tags: projects , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , claude-code , claude-mythos-fable

 They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414

 But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js.

 In eyeballing the code I find the Three.js slightly easier to understand myself, but I rarely look at the code for these 3D projects so that isn't a particularly big deal.

blogs.name: Import AI
blogs.title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

 Subscribe now

 AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem:
 …An evocative taste of the singularity…
 In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge.
 The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture.

 What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.”

 Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans.
 Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) .

 ***

 Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world:
 …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover…
 Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects – this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world.

 More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars:

 “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation,

 (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.”

 “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.”

 Why this matters – hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it – the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself.
 Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”.
 Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) .

 ***

 Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think – especially with Starship:
 …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization…
 Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write.

 Moon manufacturing – cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon.
 “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”.
 Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon – when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices.

 What you build on the moon and in what order: The basic idea here is to start by building simple things and then move up from there by launching a “sub-replicating system and evolve it toward the self-replication capability,” they write. “The objective is for the first robotic “colonists” on the Moon to fabricate a set of, say, 1700’s era machines and then to advance them steadily through the equivalent of the 1800’s, 1900’s, and finally back into the 2000’s. We argue that this can be accomplished in just a few decades”.
 The authors see this unfolding over 6 distinct manufacturing generations:

 Gen 1: Making gases, water, crude alloys, ceramics, solar cells.

 Gen 2.5: Plastics, rubbers, some chemicals.

 Gen 3 : Diversify chemicals, simple fabrics, eventually polymers.

 Gen 4: Sandwiched and other advanced material processes.

 Gen 5: Large-scale production.

 Gen 6: Makes all necessary materials, increasing sophistication, including making all electronics locally.

 What machines do you send to the moon?

 Excavators: “travel between the digging site and the resource processing site, delivering sufficient lunar regolith each hour to maintain production rates of the other assets.”

 Chemical plants for volatiles : One type will be oriented around producing gases and liquids like oxygen, hydrogen, water, hydrocarbons like methane, and solvents for industrial processes.

 Chemical plants for solids: Produce plastics and rubbers from lunar pole ice. “We now know that the ice contains large quantities of carbon molecules (CO, CO2,…) as well as nitrogen-bearing and hydrogen-bearing molecules… these materials may be needed for gaskets, seals, and insulators, for example.”

 Metal and Ceramics refining: Early generations will “produce crude ‘mongrel alloys’ by electrowinning or other methods” and hardware built out of this stuff will need to be huge to add strength to make up for poor mechanical properties. “Subsequent generations of metal refineries will add processes and material streams to improve the mechanics of the materials. Oxygen and other gases produced by metal refining will be sent to the chemistry plants”.

 Manufacturing: “Additive manufacturing will have two forms: 3D printers that make parts that are small enough to fit inside the printer, and larger units that move about robotically and add material onto large structures external to themselves”.

 Power station: The initial mass of hardware shipped to the moon will include a power station, potentially including a small nuclear reactor.

 Robonauts: Robots “will perform the assembly and maintenance tasks”. The number of robots will need to grow very rapidly to scale the industry. “Beginning with the third generation their structural components are made on the Moon, while Earth continues to send their cameras, computers, motors, and sensors. Eventually they are made completely on the Moon.” The report – which was written in 2016 – envisages teleoperation for these robonauts, though it seems likely to me that more can be done by them autonomously than first anticipated when this was written,

 Electronics manufacturing: Initially, machines will be built with electronics imported from Earth and it’ll only be possible to build very basic things, like resistors and capacitors, on the moon. As development continues it’ll get easier, eventually including having lithography machines on the moon. “The early computer chips will lack the transistor density of chips made on Earth, but they will be adequate for “appropriate technology” in space.”

 A reminder of how fast AI has moved: The report also contains some discussions around the types of AI that may be needed to operate the robots on the moon. The report – remember it was published in 2016 – includes some fun underestimates of the rate of AI progress: “On-going advances in robotic software and artificial intelligence present a very optimistic picture that these levels of robotics will be achieved as Moravec predicted, with lizard-level occurring by 2020, mouse-level by 2030, monkey-level by 2040, and human-level by 2050… Only mouse-level is needed by the end of bootstrapping on the Moon,” the report writes. By most measures, AI is around monkey-level and approaching human-level now in the 2020s.

 Why this matters – towards the industrialization of the solar system: The sooner we build industry on the moon, the sooner we’ll be able to branch out to industrialize chunks of the solar system. “After the industry becomes self-supporting it can be sent to other parts of the solar system. The asteroid belt has everything necessary for it: water, carbon, silicates, metals, oxygen, solar energy (with much larger collecting arrays), etc. The ices in the lunar poles are a limited resource so it will be important to move the center of industry to the asteroids as quickly as possible. There, the billion-fold greater resources could allow the industry to expand exponentially until it dwarfs that of the entire Earth within just a few decades,” the authors write. “When we spread robotic industry throughout the solar system, it will become the analog of Earth’s biosphere and food chain. We might call it a robotosphere. The interrelationship of robots in space may be studied by robo-ecologists learning how to optimize the robotosphere in support of humanity’s goals.”
 Read more : Affordable, Rapid Bootstrapping of the Space Industry and Solar System Civilization (arXiv) .

 ***

 Core Automation wants to stitch “compute islands” together:
 …AI startup takes a crack at distributed training…
 Core Automation, an AI startup founded by senior people from OpenAI and Google, has published a post about distributed training as well as shared details of its own attempts here. Distributed training is where you train an AI system across multiple data centers, sometimes with different types of connectivity and chips – it’s an important technology to track because the more it matures, the more people can have a shot at building...

blogs.content:
Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 9,830 new readers. A week ago, Nvidia was brushing off a report about an alleged spy plot involving its CEO as routine customer meetings. Now, Jensen Huang is publicly apologizing, and his own board is investigating.
 Few founders are as inseparable from what they built as Huang, and no company touches the entire global AI industry like Nvidia. So the fallout from his admitted affair could reach far beyond a single boardroom.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims

 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk

 Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 NVIDIA
 🕵️ Jensen Huang admits affair as Nvidia probes spy claims
 Image source: NetThunder on LinkedIn

 The Rundown: Nvidia’s board of directors just ordered an independent review of reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a “foreign intelligence effort,” with Huang admitting to an extramarital affair in a letter to staff and saying, “There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
 The details:
 Sec. of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw a spring memo on Jensen and Alice Huang, an Nvidia customer exec it linked to China’s top spy agency.

 After calling their meetings “completely normal” last month, Jensen told staff, “I was unfaithful to my wife” and reportedly confirmed the relationship to the board.

 Reporting has yet to establish what, if anything, Ms. Huang (aka Huang Le, no relation to Jensen) learned from him, while China denies the spying claims.

 Outside lawyers and independent directors will run the review as Jensen stays CEO, with the board seeing “no reason to believe” any secrets were compromised.

 Jensen also has until Nov. 11 to answer a House GOP request for a private briefing, with more congressional investigations expected over the relationship.

 Why it matters: AI stocks are already reeling from the midterm election results. Now, a spy scandal around the CEO of one of the industry’s biggest companies is unlikely to help either. Nvidia touches nearly every aspect of the AI industry, and Huang is the frontman of it all, so all eyes will be on what the board finds and his future with Nvidia.

 TOGETHER WITH GARTNER
 🔮  How can you predict IT workforce needs?  

 The Rundown: AI is accelerating how fast skills become obsolete, making future workforce needs nearly impossible to predict. This Gartner webinar explores three planning traps and offers a framework for building a resilient IT workforce.
 In this webinar, you'll learn how to:
 Avoid common workforce planning traps

 Separate enduring from transient skills

 Align talent with long-term value

 Register today .

 THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE
 💡  The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.
 Brooke, Community Lead: I'm on the customer side, not the engineering side. When something breaks, I usually find out when a customer writes in, and by then a bunch of people have already hit it. We had an error chart in our analytics tool, but I don't often remember to check that dashboard every day, and a basic “alert me over X errors” setup would go off constantly for things that aren't real problems.
 I built a Claude scheduled task that checks our error chart every morning, filters out the noise, and tells the whole team in Slack only when something's actually wrong. I set it up just by describing what I wanted in plain English. I gave Claude the rules on which error types are real problems and which aren't, and it only counts the ones that matter.
 Now, I hear about issues before customers have to tell me. I tested it over the past couple of weeks, and it flagged every day something really broke and stayed silent on a busy day that was all harmless errors.
 Jennifer, Tech & Robotics Writer: My preteen daughter has spent months debating whether or not to get bangs, mostly worried about the "total humiliation" if they went wrong. So we uploaded her photo to ChatGPT and asked for four versions of bangs: blunt, curtain, wispy, side-swept.
 She loved it and finally narrowed down her choice, and the appointment is booked for this weekend. It’s hardly a groundbreaking use case, but it’s a fun way to try on a decision before a stylist makes it permanent.

 AI TRAINING
 🔖  Turn your X bookmarks into a personal research desk

 The Rundown: X moves quickly, and saving posts is easy. Finding the useful ideas again is harder. In this guide, you’ll connect Grok Bot to X, review a week of bookmarks, spot repeated themes, and turn one finding into a post draft.
 Step-by-step:
 Check the difference between free Grok chat and Grok Bot. Bot is included with Premium, Super, and Ultra on the X Subscription. X Chat is still rolling out

 Connect the official X plugin with the Grok Bot. Check that it is linked to the same account where you save posts

 Bookmark 8 to 12 useful posts about one topic. Choose examples, questions, and problems, not just launch announcements

 Message your Bot in X Chat and ask it to group the bookmarks into themes. Check the direct links and compare each claim with the original post

 Choose one supported theme and ask for an X post draft. Review the wording and sources yourself; leave publishing off

 Pro tip: A set of bookmarks can show what you have been reading, but it can’t prove what all of X thinks. Keep the source links with every theme.

 PRESENTED BY OPENART
 💡   Create a launch video for your business

 The Rundown: Need a launch video for your business? Simply paste your website link, add your brand assets, and define your target audience. OpenArt's AI video agent will shape the story and messaging while handling the script, motion design, voiceover, and video editing.
 With OpenArt, you can:
 Turn your website, screenshots, or pitch deck into a launch video

 Create short promos or longer videos to showcase your business

 Refine scenes, voiceovers, or music by describing the changes

 Go beyond launches with product ads and UGC-style videos

 Create your launch video with OpenArt.

 ANTHROPIC
 💤  Anthropic’s Claude ‘dreams’ to fix its own memory
 Image source: Anthropic

 The Rundown: Anthropic just published its own take on AI “dreaming,” sharing how Claude agents use downtime to fix and reorganize their memory, and what it’s learned about what an AI should actually bother remembering.
 The details:
 Memory refers to notes Claude saves as files and reads back in later sessions, so it can build on past work instead of starting from scratch each time.

 Unlike ChatGPT’s version, which previously built a profile of the user, Anthropic’s dreaming has Claude check its notes against logs of past work to catch errors.

 Anthropic said newer models have gotten much better at judging what to save, and that explaining to the AI why memory matters beats rules on what to write.

 In tests on Pokémon, Fable 5 earned four badges with only 10 memory files, while an older Sonnet 3.7 got just one using 413, and Opus 5.5 beat the game entirely.

 Why it matters: It feels like not too long ago that the early iterations of ‘memory’ in AI assistants were a comically simple scratchpad with bare-bones notes on the user. Now they can recall past chats in detail down to the most obscure reference, and the next step is agents that continuously remember the job and improve at it the longer they work.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Kate built a custom camera feature for Facebook Live presentations
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Kate MacGregor :
 “I built a live camera bubble that floats over my slides during Facebook Live presentations. Because Facebook Live does not let me switch between my camera and a shared screen, I wanted my face to stay visible while I presented. This is useful for anyone who streams presentations to a Facebook Group and wants viewers to see them speaking.
 Claude Code built the working app within about five minutes. I made one tweak to the camera bubble's shape, and it was then a finished, usable product.
 When I'm ready to go live in the Facebook Group, I click the camera bubble app on my local desktop. It uses my laptop camera, and I can drag the bubble around the screen and choose the circle size that suits whatever I'm sharing. Before I go live, I select "share entire screen" in the Facebook Live settings. Viewers then see my slides or screen with my floating camera bubble, so they can see me speaking as I present.”

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: When Does the US Become a Net Importer of Tokens?
blogs.description: Read on tomtunguz.com → With AI demand outpacing supply, & domestic data center construction slowing, soon the US will consume more tokens…
blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 With AI demand outpacing supply, & domestic data center construction slowing, soon the US will consume more tokens than it produces.

 At that point, the US will become a net importer of tokens, just like it is a net importer of rare earth metals. A basic model estimates this switch between 2028 & 2030, depending on how many planned facilities get cancelled.

 Very roughly, the current systems, with new data centers coming online, can manage 2.5x annual token growth 1 . Above that rate, chip & model efficiency gains can no longer offset domestic demand growth : power required in gigawatts equals tokens demanded divided by tokens per watt.

 If 45% of planned projects fail to connect, imports start by 2028. Cut cancellations to 20%, & the deadline slips to 2029. Even if every proposed facility gets built on time, the gap still opens by 2030 2 .

 Every physical model assumes the price of compute stays constant. In reality, when supply chokes, prices spike. So far, demand has proven remarkably price-inelastic. Over the past two quarters, short-term GPU rental prices surged from $5 to more than $13 per hour 3 , Anthropic signed billions in burst compute at premium rates, & overall demand barely blinked. Buyers simply paid the toll.

 At what price do people balk? Is it the model labs burning through capital to pre-train the next frontier? The enterprises financing vibe-coding teams that burn hundreds of millions of tokens a week building custom apps? Or consumers asked to pay $40 a month for an autonomous agent subscription?

 Surely there is some price at which demand will slow & current data center capacity will suffice. But throttling demand through scarcity pricing denies the basic market reality : at a lower cost of production, demand would be orders of magnitude higher. If we do not build the domestic power and facilities to satisfy that demand, tokens will simply be produced elsewhere & imported.

 The uninhibited growth since GPT 3.5 will be modulated not by lack of access to data, nor algorithmic limits, nor GPU manufacturing speed, but by the broader values of the country. The forthcoming limits on the quantity, size, electrical consumption, & location of data centers will reshape Startupland.

---

 Demand grows from a 66gw base in 2027, up 61% from 41gw (Goldman Sachs Commodities Research, Wei, Struyven & Dart, May 20, 2026. US data center power 31gw / 41gw / 66gw for 2025 / 2026 / 2027). Efficiency is the counterweight. Tokens per watt compounds about 2.9x a year, blending NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin at 5.4x over GB300, Google’s Ironwood at 2x Trillium & AWS’s Trainium3 at 4x Trainium2 (SemiAnalysis InferenceX, 2026 : Vera Rubin 5.4x GB300 on tokens per watt. NVIDIA claims up to 10x on agentic workloads. Google TPU Ironwood 2x Trillium. AWS Trainium3 4x Trainium2). Supply is the third input, & only 55% of scheduled US capacity lands on time.  ↩︎

 The chart is a capacity date, not an economic one. Power is only 5% of the cost of a GPU-hour ; capital recovery is 64%. A $40/mwh spread is worth $0.35b per gigawatt per year, while a 6%-to-9% cost of capital spread is worth $0.84b. Capital wins. Latency finishes the argument : New York to Frankfurt round-trips in 88ms. Behind-the-meter generation covers much of the shortfall, so the real constraint becomes gas turbines, sold out into 2030 (SemiAnalysis, June 25, 2026 ; GE Vernova, July 22, 2026).  ↩︎

 Tomasz Tunguz, The Financial Engineering Essential for AI in 2027 , November 3, 2026, analyzing Anthropic’s Form S-1/A disclosures on short-term burst compute surges to $12–$13/GPU-hour (up from $3–$5 six months earlier) and long-term compute commitments. The Ornn Compute Index settled at $12.29/GPU-hour in October 2026.  ↩︎

blogs.title: Jensen Huang’s Affair, The Culper Report, Huang’s Righteousness
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese spy, and that might not be the end of his troubles. I hope he survives, but his influence will never be the same.
blogs.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Chinese spy, and that might not be the end of his troubles. I hope he survives, but his influence will never be the same.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I discussed the voters’ opposition to data centers, and the current state of Google. Then, on Sunday’s subscriber mailbag , we discussed Andrew’s reflection on X’s impact on the election , Bending Spoons, and more.

On to the Update, as the news continues to defeat my attempt to have any sort of schedule (or catch up on earnings).

Jensen Huang’s Affair

From Bloomberg :

Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy, plunging the chip colossus into a crisis like none before in its three-decade history. Huang disclosed the romantic relationship in a memo to employees on Sunday, saying the Nvidia board was launching an investigation. He had previously said there was nothing inappropriate about his relationship with the woman, who worked for a Singapore-based customer.

It was a humbling moment for an executive who became one of Silicon Valley’s biggest celebrities in recent years. Huang has crisscrossed the globe promoting artificial intelligence computing — a field his company dominates — drawing throngs of fans swept up in “Jensanity.” His relentless appearances, featuring science lectures, dad jokes and his signature leather jackets, have turned him into AI’s main cheerleader.

The incident also threatens to further roil an AI market shaken by concerns about a slowdown in data center spending. Nvidia makes chips that are crucial to AI computing equipment and is one of the world’s most valuable businesses. Turmoil within the company threatens to reverberate through the broader industry. Nvidia has emerged as a key source of financing for AI infrastructure as well. Huang has worked with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms on a $500 billion effort to help companies rapidly build out their equipment, and he’s funneled money into bolstering the AI supply chain and fledgling customers.

That’s a good overview of the stakes: it’s not just Nvidia products, but also Nvidia financing . Meanwhile, the most prominent in those “series of reports” was this New York Times article :

Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the highly classified memo this past spring warning top Trump administration officials that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy, multiple people briefed on the matter said. The document was based on classified intelligence from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen who was a senior executive at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia’s advanced artificial intelligence chips and being investigated for illegally smuggling them into China. U.S. officials had concluded that Ms. Huang was in a close relationship with the Nvidia chief, who is no relation, and that she had been recruited to spy by China’s top intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security…

Despite his status as an A.I. pioneer and head of one of the world’s most valuable companies, Mr. Huang was initially left off the list of major business and tech executives invited to join Mr. Trump in China. It is unclear whether the exclusion was connected to the memo. By that point, a number of people inside the administration were concerned about Mr. Huang’s influence on the president’s policy of only lightly regulating A.I., people briefed on the matter said…

This strikes me as the most important paragraph. First, it was odd that Huang wasn’t invited on the trip; second, it was notable that Trump made a big deal out of inviting him anyways; third, I think we have our best clue as far as who is the most interested in this news becoming public, and it’s not necessarily China. Continuing with the story:

The president chose at that point not to take any action. He has viewed Nvidia’s chips as integral to America’s competition with China in A.I. He sees Nvidia’s success as crucial to maintaining a robust stock market. Asked about Mr. Huang’s admission to his company about his affair with Ms. Huang, Mr. Trump told reporters on Sunday evening that he did not regret his own lack of action. “No, I don’t think so,” the president said. He added that he believed Mr. Huang should stay on as Nvidia’s chief executive. “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” Mr. Trump said.

Huang didn’t offer much of an excuse in an email to all Nvidia employees:

To my colleagues at NVIDIA,

I owe my family and all of you an apology.

I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.

To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.

To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.

Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.

My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.

Jensen

The Board of Directors issued a statement:

The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation.

The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.

While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.

Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.

The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.

Quite a Sunday — and if this news were contained to just this Sunday, then this would all probably blow over. But it’s not.

The Culper Report

In May a short seller named Culper Research published a report and a thread on X that was focused on Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed, the firm that Alice Huang worked for:

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA. We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. https://t.co/oTaJyL7S2R

— Culper (@CulperResearch) May 13, 2026

This was the 9th post in the thread:

From the report:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, a Chinese national. He was first spotted partying with Alice Huang in June 2024 – the same month the Apex/Alibaba pledge was filed. He then dined with Alice Huang in Taiwan in May 2025 – just weeks after the news of U.S. trade restrictions. Finally, per one current Megaspeed employee, Jensen visits Megaspeed-linked data centers “every few months” and “every single time” he visits, he is accompanied by representatives from Alibaba. The Megaspeed employee characterized their relationship with Jensen as “very close”, corroborating another former Nvidia employee’s suggestion to us that many Nvidia employees wondered if there was a special relationship. The same employee added that, in contrast to public reporting suggesting otherwise, Alice Huang is “actually still our boss.”…

In October 2025, Nvidia partner YTL AI Cloud opened a $4.3 billion data center in Johor, Malaysia, housing Blackwell-equipped servers. A current Megaspeed employee told us that Megaspeed is “one of the most important customers” for YTL, but that the parties conceal the relationship, saying, “Megaspeed is able to get the supply of the GPUs and supply to the Chinese companies. They don’t want the media attention so that it doesn’t disrupt their business plans in the data centers.”

There is more to the report than just Alice Huang, but the primary focus is Megaspeed in support of Culper’s contention that Nvidia actually still has a sizable China business and is very much aware of that fact. It’s pretty damning.

---

Presented by

Agentic commerce purchases with Link, Stripe’s digital wallet that works surprisingly well for agents, grew 38x in September. The catalyst was consumer agents like Muse and Instinct.

I’ve recently written about how these platforms are enabling agents to do genuinely useful things on our behalf. When one of those things is spending money, it needs a wallet that knows what it is, and isn’t, allowed to do.

Stripe, in building Link, has learned that’s really about deciding how much freedom to give it. You might approve one purchase, or give it $500 for flights this week, and let it figure out the rest. The wallet’s job is to keep it within those lines while handling everything between “go buy this” and the purchase actually happening.

You can use Link on Muse, Instinct, as well as many other of the agents you might use already.

---

Huang’s Righteousness

As news of this scandal seeped out over the weekend, I was pretty put off by tweets from China hawks strongly insinuating that Huang’s (then) rumored affair explained his push to sell chips to China, as if Huang would normally have agreed with them but was betraying the country because of who he was sleeping with. I think this is completely wrong.

The fact of the matter is that it is entirely rational — and defensible — for Nvidia to want to sell chips to China (an argument I have made repeatedly ). From an Nvidia-specific perspective, selling chips to China is critical for maintaining the CUDA software moat; if China can’t use Nvidia chips, then it will be motivated by necessity to build an alternative, and that alternative is not going to stay in China: it will, in the long run, be an alternative to CUDA around the world. This is no small thing: it’s Huang’s life’s work, and one of Nvidia’s most important differentiators.

From a U.S. perspective, meanwhile, a similar motivation exists: as long as Chinese companies have access to Nvidia chips they have much less motivation to develop the software infrastructure and feedback mechanisms necessary for Chinese alternatives to come to market. Yes, the central government and Huawei are pushing to do just that, but chips are such a hard problem that you need “pull” as well as “push”, and Chinese AI companies are focused on building competitive models, not on national science projects (this is why China is itself not allowing the sale of Nvidia chips into China).

I think both of these points are valid, and I also have more overarching concerns about banning chips for China given our reliance on Taiwan . This is a close question, to be clear! I completely understand and could, if presse...
